fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because almost all of my own work has been on the knowledge-work side. Things like software engineering agents, web agents, that whole family. And the honest answer is that the two are different along a few axes that people tend to blur together.

The first axis is just where the environment lives. For knowledge work, the environment is digital. It's a codebase, a browser, a document, a spreadsheet. That means I can snapshot it, reset it, run a thousand copies in parallel, and the cost of a failed attempt is basically compute. That's enormously important for evaluation, because it means you can actually iterate. With construction, the environment is the world. You can't reset a half-poured foundation. Every trial is slow, expensive, and in some cases dangerous, so you end up evaluating on a tiny number of episodes, or you evaluate in simulation and then pray the sim-to-real gap is small.

The second axis is verification, and here I think the intuition people have is actually backwards. People assume physical tasks are harder to grade. But if you build a wall, the wall is either level or it isn't, it either bears load or it doesn't. The physics gives you a very unforgiving ground truth. Knowledge work is often the fuzzier one. With something like SWE-bench we got lucky, because software has tests, so you get a crisp signal. But most knowledge work isn't like that. If I ask a model to write a strategy memo or do a literature review, what's the test? You end up with human raters or model-based judges, and now your evaluation has its own error rate and its own biases. So the hard part on the knowledge side isn't collecting episodes, it's defining what good even means.

The third axis is what failure looks like. In a digital task, the agent can take a bad action and then recover. It can undo an edit, re-run a command, backtrack. Physical tasks are often irreversible at a very fine grain, so the premium on getting it right the first time is much higher, and your evaluation has to care about the trajectory, not just the final state.

And then the last thing I'd say is about data. The reason language models got good at knowledge work is that the internet is a giant log of knowledge work. Text in, text out. There is no comparable log of a plumber's hands. So when people ask why we have coding agents but not construction robots, it's not really that one task is intellectually harder. It's that one of them came with a training set and a test harness almost for free, and the other has to have both built from scratch.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see the difference is to ask two questions about any task. How hard is it to define what success looks like? And how expensive is it to actually run the test?

For knowledge work, running the test is cheap. Everything lives in a digital environment. You can snapshot it, reset it, run the same task a thousand times, and run it in parallel. That's what made benchmarks like SWE-bench possible. You take a real GitHub issue, let the model try to fix it, and run the repository's unit tests. The environment is fully reproducible, and you get a signal in minutes. The hard part is defining success. Software is a lucky case because tests give you a partial ground truth. But think about writing a legal memo, doing a financial analysis, or handling a customer service conversation. What counts as good becomes fuzzy, it depends on context, and people often disagree. A lot of our recent work, like tau-bench, has been about how you evaluate an agent that has to talk to a user, follow a policy, and use tools, all at the same time. You also care about reliability, not just whether the agent succeeded once. If you run it eight times, does it succeed eight times? That's what matters if you're going to deploy it.

Physical tasks like construction are almost the reverse. In many cases, defining success is fairly concrete. Is the wall plumb? Does the joint hold? Did the structure pass inspection? Running the test is the brutal part. You can't reset a construction site. Actions are often irreversible: once you pour concrete or cut a beam, you're committed. Every trial costs real time and material, and it carries safety risk. So instead of thousands of trials, you might get a handful. That makes statistically meaningful evaluation very hard. Simulation helps, but there's always the sim-to-real gap. Real sites are messy and unstructured. The lighting changes, materials vary, and other people and machines are moving around. A system that looks great in simulation can fall apart because of something no one thought to model.

There's also a question of time horizon and of how much of the task is visible. A lot of knowledge work, even long-horizon tasks, can be broken into checkable steps. Construction unfolds over weeks or months, and the quality of early steps sometimes only shows up much later. A foundation problem might not reveal itself until you're three floors up. So you need evaluation that tracks intermediate states, not just final outcomes.

The last thing I'd say is that physical evaluation will probably end up looking more like how we evaluate human tradespeople. That means certification, supervised apprenticeship, graduated levels of autonomy, and ongoing inspection, rather than a single leaderboard number. Honestly, I think knowledge-work evaluation is heading in that direction too. As models get more capable, static benchmarks saturate quickly. We'll need to evaluate these systems more like we evaluate colleagues: on sustained, reliable performance in realistic settings, with humans in the loop. The physical world just forces you to confront that reality sooner, because the cost of getting it wrong is so visible.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot because so much of my work has been on building evaluations and benchmarks for AI systems.

For knowledge work, the thing that makes evaluation tractable is that the entire task lives in a digital environment. If I want to test whether a model can fix a bug in a codebase, or handle a customer service request, or write an analysis, the inputs and outputs are all text or code or structured data. That means I can run the task thousands of times, I can check the output automatically — does the code pass the tests, did the agent follow the policy — and I can iterate very quickly. That's really why we've seen such fast progress on things like software engineering: the feedback loop between "try something" and "know whether it worked" is incredibly tight, and the cost of a failure during evaluation is basically zero.

Physical tasks like construction break almost all of those assumptions. First, there's no cheap way to run the experiment. If I want to know whether a robot can frame a wall or install plumbing, I either need the actual robot in an actual building — which is slow and expensive — or I need a simulator, and our simulators are still quite far from capturing the messiness of the real world: friction, deformable materials, dust, things breaking in ways you didn't model. Second, the success criteria are much harder to specify. "Did the code compile" is a crisp signal; "is this wall built correctly" involves tolerances, safety codes, judgment calls that even humans partially learn through apprenticeship rather than written specs. And third, the cost of failure is real — a mistake in the physical world can damage property or hurt someone, so you can't just let the system fail its way to competence the way we do with language models.

So my mental model is: for knowledge work, we're mostly limited by how well we can design the benchmark — making it realistic, making sure it's not contaminated, capturing the long-horizon nature of real jobs. For physical work, we're limited by something more fundamental, which is that evaluation itself requires interacting with the physical world, and we haven't figured out how to make that fast, cheap, and safe. That asymmetry, I think, explains a lot about why AI is transforming digital professions first, and it's also why I suspect progress on physical tasks will look different — more gradual, more tied to hardware and data collection infrastructure, rather than the kind of rapid scaling we've seen with language.

opus-5.text:
It's a really interesting asymmetry, and I think it cuts in the opposite direction from what people expect.

The intuition is usually that physical tasks are harder to evaluate because the world is messy. But actually the world is a *fantastic* grader. If you ask a system to frame a wall, the wall is either plumb or it isn't. You put a level on it. The load is carried or the thing sags. There's no debate about the rubric. Whereas in a lot of knowledge work — write me a memo, summarize this deposition, design this schema — what does success even mean? We end up asking a language model to grade another language model, and now your evaluation signal is only as good as your judge, and the judge has all the same blind spots as the thing being judged. That's a genuinely uncomfortable place to be scientifically.

So in knowledge work, data is nearly free and verification is the bottleneck. In physical work, verification is nearly free and *data* is the bottleneck. You can't run ten thousand parallel rollouts on a construction site. You can't reset the state — if the robot pours the slab wrong, you don't get to try again cheaply. And there's a safety constraint that means you can't do the kind of wide, dumb exploration that made a lot of our RL successes work.

The other thing I'd flag is that construction is almost pathologically non-stationary. Every site is different soil, different weather, different crew, different inspector. The tacit knowledge a good foreman has is enormous and mostly undocumented — it's not in any corpus we can train on. In knowledge work we got lucky: people had already written down a staggering fraction of what they know.

The place I think these converge is long-horizon tasks. Once you're evaluating something that takes a model a week of work rather than thirty seconds, knowledge work starts to look a lot more like a construction project — lots of interdependent steps, failures that only show up much later, and the hard question of how you assign credit across all of it. We don't really have good evaluation methodology for that yet, in either domain.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference is how cheap it is to try something, check it, and try again.

Knowledge work happens in a digital medium. The model reads text, writes code, or fills out a spreadsheet, and the output is an artifact I can inspect. Sometimes I can verify it automatically, like running unit tests on code. Even when I can't, I can run thousands of attempts in parallel, reset the environment for free, and iterate quickly. That's a big reason the field moved so fast on language and coding. The training and the evaluation both live in the same world.

Physical tasks like construction break almost all of those assumptions. You need a body or a robot, a real environment, and real physics. Failure has a cost: a mistake can break something, or hurt someone. You can't reset a half-built wall with a keystroke. Simulation helps, but the sim-to-real gap is large, because the world is messy in ways that are hard to model. Materials behave differently, lighting changes, a site isn't laid out like the last one, and a lot of the expertise is tacit. A good tradesperson has intuition they couldn't write down.

The success criteria are also different. In knowledge work, we're often asking whether the answer is right or useful. In construction, the question is whether the thing is built to spec, safe, and up to code, and that might only show up months later. It's also a long-horizon, multi-party process, with sequencing, coordination, and handling surprises.

So I'd say evaluation is harder for physical tasks, and it's also much more expensive and slower. Even for knowledge work, though, I don't think we're done. Benchmarks saturate, and real work is far messier than a clean test. We should be careful about assuming our digital evaluations tell us much about how well AI would do out in the physical world.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference is what feedback looks like. When we evaluate a model on knowledge work, the output is usually text or code, and we can check it fairly cheaply. We can run tests, compare against a reference, or have someone read it in a few minutes. The environment is also close to the one the model was trained on, so the failure modes are fairly legible.

Physical tasks are different in a few ways. The environment is continuous and only partly observed, so a plan that looks sound on paper can fail because of a detail nobody modeled, like a surface that isn't quite level or a fitting that doesn't line up. Errors also compound over many steps and can be expensive or dangerous to undo. And evaluation is much harder to scale. You often need a simulator, and then you have to ask how well that simulator matches the real world, which is its own research problem.

So I'd be careful about treating progress on knowledge benchmarks as a proxy for construction-like competence. Reasoning well about a building plan on a page is useful, but it's a different skill from carrying that plan out with a robot on a job site. The honest way to measure the second is to build evaluations that look more like the real task, with humans in the loop for the parts that carry real risk.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things to separate: how hard a task is to do, and how hard it is to tell whether it was done well. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

With knowledge work, the output might be a document, a piece of code, or a recommendation. Some of those have fairly concrete checks—you can run code and see whether it passes a test. But if you’re asking whether a recommendation is useful, you need to know the context, what the person wanted, and perhaps what happened after they followed it. Just producing something that looks reasonable isn’t enough.

With construction, you have a physical outcome and constraints you can measure. But that doesn’t make evaluation trivial. Something can look finished and still have problems that only show up later. And testing in the physical world can be expensive, with consequences you can’t simply reset.

So I’d want evaluations in both settings to connect to actual outcomes: did the system accomplish the task, under the relevant constraints, and how much human intervention did it need?

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two separate questions: how do you judge whether the work was done well, and how hard is it to actually run the evaluation?

For knowledge work, you can often run evaluations very cheaply. You can give a system a thousand problems and collect its answers. But deciding whether those answers are useful can be difficult. If it’s writing code, you might have tests. If it’s writing a strategy document, there may be several good answers, and the quality depends on what the person asking actually needs.

With construction, you have a physical outcome that you can inspect and measure. But evaluating the process is much more expensive. You need the environment, the materials, and some way of interacting with them. And a mistake can damage something or hurt someone. You can’t necessarily just reset and try again.

So I wouldn’t say one is uniformly easier to evaluate. In digital tasks, the challenge is often specifying what success means. In physical tasks, even when you can specify success, collecting evidence that the system can achieve it reliably across different situations is a substantial challenge.

sol-5.6.text:
I think the key difference is that, in knowledge work, the artifact and the evaluation often live in the same digital world. If an AI writes code, for example, you can run tests; if it summarizes a document, a person can inspect the output. You can evaluate millions of attempts relatively cheaply and quickly.

Physical tasks are much less forgiving. In construction, success depends not only on knowing what to do, but on perception, dexterity, materials, sequencing, safety, and all the unexpected things that happen on a real site. A system that is right 95 percent of the time may look impressive on a knowledge benchmark, but a robot that drops a beam 5 percent of the time is unusable. So the evaluation has to measure reliability, recovery from mistakes, and performance over long horizons—not just whether the final answer looks correct.

luna-5.6.text:
I think the distinction is less about whether the task is “intellectual” or “manual” and more about the structure of the feedback. In knowledge work, an AI system can often operate in a relatively clean digital environment, produce an artifact, and be evaluated against examples or outcomes. Construction is embodied, long-horizon, and highly contingent: the system has to perceive a changing physical environment, coordinate tools and people, deal with uncertainty, and maintain safety over many sequential decisions. A small mistake can compound or create real costs.

So for construction, evaluation needs to measure more than task completion. We would want to look at reliability, adaptability, recovery from errors, physical dexterity, collaboration, and safety under novel conditions. It is also important to compare systems to the full cost of human labor and supervision, not just to a benchmark score. A system that performs impressively in a controlled demonstration may still be far from being useful on a real job site.

Physical tasks have to be judged in the world. A construction task, for example, involves materials, tools, timing, coordination, and safety, and success means the job actually gets done to the required standard. So you need to evaluate not just what a system can say, but how reliably it can act under real constraints and recover when things don’t go as planned.
